Before the first dawn, the world was a black bowl filled with sleeping water. In its center floated Nara, a small turtle with a shell of plain stone. She was lonely, so she tapped her shell against the dark. Each tap became a star, but the stars were cold and far away.

Nara dove to the bottom of the water and found a coal hidden in the mud. She carried it upward in her mouth, though it burned her tongue. When she reached the surface, she placed the coal upon her back. The stone shell cracked with heat, and golden light poured through the cracks.

The light woke the sky. It stretched itself wide and blue. The waters, seeing the brightness, began to dance, and their waves became hills, rivers, and forests. Where sparks fell from Nara’s shell, birds rose singing. Where her tears fell, people appeared, warm and wondering.

But Nara grew tired. She sank beneath the new earth to rest. Even now, when the ground trembles, elders say she is turning in her sleep, making sure the coal still burns and the world remembers the brave turtle who carried fire through darkness for everyone above.

Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of dark water, and all creatures slept beneath its surface. Only Nara, the little fire-moth, was awake. She saw the sleeping mountains curled like turtles and the forests dreaming green dreams, but there was no light to wake them.

Nara flew upward until she found the Sky Giant, who kept the sun hidden inside a bronze jar. “Light is too bright for the young world,” he rumbled. “It will frighten everything.”

“But without it,” Nara said, “nothing will know its own name.”

The giant laughed, and his breath blew Nara against the jar. Her wings struck the bronze, and a single spark fell out. She caught it in her mouth, though it burned her tongue, and carried it down to the water.

When the spark touched the sea, it became dawn. Mountains lifted their heads. Trees opened their leaves. Birds burst from the waves, singing the names of things.

Nara’s wings were scorched brown forever, but every morning her children dance near lamps and fires, remembering the brave moth who stole the first light so the world could wake and recognize itself. And each sunrise is her kiss upon the sky.

Myth: Before the first morning, the world was a deep black lake, and every mountain, tree, and creature slept beneath its glassy skin. Only Nara, the fire-moth, stirred in the dark. She fluttered over the silent waters, longing to see the faces of the dreams below.

Far above, the Sky Giant guarded a bronze jar sealed with thunder. Inside it burned the first sun. “The world is too young for light,” he warned. “It will shatter what still sleeps.”

Nara answered, “What sleeps forever is never born.”

She struck the jar with her fragile wings. Once, twice, seven times she beat against the bronze until a bright coal slipped free. It scorched her mouth as she carried it downward, but she did not let it fall.

When Nara touched the coal to the lake, dawn spilled across the waters. Mountains rose like waking beasts. Forests shook out their leaves. Birds flew from golden foam, singing names into the air. Last came people, blinking, with warmth in their hands.

Nara’s wings remained darkened at the edges. That is why moths still circle flames, not from foolishness, but to greet their ancient mother, who taught the world to wake. Every sunrise repeats her promise of light.

When her task was done, Nara sank beneath the land to rest, the ember glowing on her back. Earthquakes, elders say, are only Nara turning gently, guarding the first fire, so dawn will always find its way home.
